content:
# Red-Team: Deniable-yet-Verifiable Comms in the Frontier-Scout Burn Pipeline

## Scope and threat model (fixed, so the attacks below are well-defined)

Protocol claims: (1) **Deniability** — covertext is recoverable *only* with the codebook; observers without it learn nothing, including that anything is hidden. (2) **Authorship** — a designated verifier set can prove who sent a recovered message. (3) **Burn** — artifacts are destroyed post-consumption. Attackers: passive observer, active injector, captured scout, partial-material insider, compelled-disclosure adversary, compromised base.

Two axioms the whole scheme hangs on. Every bypass below targets a violation of one of them:

- **Axiom 1 — Partitioned verifiability.** Public-verifiable non-repudiation and outsider-deniability are mutually exclusive on the same artifact. Verifier material must be secret and held only by the base. Anything publicly checkable is a beacon.
- **Axiom 2 — Fail-closed determinism.** Every mitigation must be a CI assertion or a runtime invariant, not a guideline. If it isn't machine-enforced, assume it's absent.

---

## Class A — Detecting the channel (deniability broken without recovery)

**1. Statistical embedding fingerprints.** Naive stego (LSBs, timing jitter, padding choices) shifts the cover distribution; learned steganalysis picks it up without ever recovering content.
**Mitigation:** Choice-encoding. Covers are emitted by the *genuine* ambient traffic generator; the payload selects *which* generator output is sent. Every emitted cover is a fully valid sample of the ambient process — KL divergence between emitted and ambient distributions is zero by construction. Where free-form embedding is unavoidable, encode via arithmetic coding under a cover model fitted to live ambient traffic, refreshed weekly.

**2. Length/volume correlation.** Payload size maps to cover size; traffic analysis recovers message size and cadence.
**Mitigation:** Quantize every payload to fixed size buckets (next power of two, PRF-padded). Emit constant-volume epochs: idle periods carry PRF-generated decoy covers so total bytes per epoch is load-independent. Enforced by a wire-format invariant: decoder rejects any non-canonical length.

**3. Timing correlation / silence-as-signal.** Send-on-event reveals event times; silence after a major event is itself intelligence.
**Mitigation:** Slotted emission. Scouts transmit only at fixed slots (or Poisson with parameters identical to background chatter), buffering real payloads; empty slots carry decoys. Event information lives in content, never in cadence. Runtime invariant: emission timestamps are slot-quantized, independent of event timestamps.

**4. Carrier and transport outliers.** Rare file types, odd ports, non-standard TLS fingerprints flag the scout regardless of content.
**Mitigation:** Carrier whitelist restricted to types ≥ threshold frequency in ambient traffic; transport pinned to a mainstream client fingerprint (stock library version, domain-fronted HTTPS). CI test asserts the deployed fingerprint string equals the pinned release.

**5. Validity-correlated receiver behavior.** Receiver ACKs valid messages, silently drops invalid ones → attacker uses the receiver as a forgery-testing oracle.
**Mitigation:** Uniform-response policy. ACKs are implicit in the next scheduled traffic stream and statistically identical whether or not a valid message arrived. No observable receiver state change may correlate with validity — asserted by differential testing on the receiver harness.

---

## Class B — Recovering content without the codebook

**6. Keystream/pad reuse.** Any repeated pad segment turns the channel into running-key cipher: C₁⊕C₂ = P₁⊕P₂. One leaked plaintext strips every overlapping message.
**Mitigation:** Information-theoretic one-time pad under a ratchet: Kᵢ = HKDF(Kᵢ₋₁, nonceᵢ, "burn"); Kᵢ₋₁ zeroized on derivation. Nonces strictly monotonic; nonce collision triggers deterministic abort and out-of-band rotation. Deliberate consequence: recorded covertext stays safe against *unbounded* adversaries forever — residual risk collapses to key custody alone.

**7. Static codebook table inference.** A literal lookup-table codebook used repeatedly is recoverable from enough (cover, context) pairs.
**Mitigation:** The "codebook" is a keyed PRF family, not a table: encodeᵢ(m) = StegoEnc(HKDF(K_master, i), m). Per-message derived encoding; finite samples don't extrapolate. Hard cap of 2²⁰ messages per master key, deterministic forced rotation, master rotated out-of-band quarterly.

**8. Weak RNG on the scout.** Predictable pads/nonnes = recovery without the codebook.
**Mitigation:** Hybrid derivation: nonce = SHA256(TRNG ∥ epoch ∥ counter). TRNG health checks gate transmission — failed health check means deterministic hold, never fallback to software entropy. Min-entropy floor asserted in CI test vectors.

**9. Cross-protocol key reuse.** Codebook material reused elsewhere creates cross-protocol oracles.
**Mitigation:** Mandatory domain-separation labels in every HKDF call; distinct label per protocol role. Lint gate rejects any HKDF invocation missing a label; labels registry is closed.

---

## Class C — Forging or subverting authorship

**10. Cut-and-paste re-embedding.** Attacker lifts a validly signed codeword and re-embeds it in a new carrier/context ("advance to grid X" replayed months later).
**Mitigation:** Sign the full context tuple: SHA256(carrier-invariant bytes) ∥ epoch ∥ seq ∥ src-id ∥ dst-id ∥ payload-hash. Carrier hash is defined over the carrier regions *not* used for embedding, computed identically pre/post-embedding — resolves the sign-then-embed ordering circularity. Receiver verifies every field against current expected values; any mismatch → deterministic drop.

**11. Splice / truncate / reorder.** Multi-frame messages disassembled and recombined.
**Mitigation:** Per-frame signature covering (epoch, seq, frame-index, total-frames, chunk). Assembly requires complete, contiguous, single-source sets; any gap or duplicate outside the anti-replay window kills the entire message.

**12. Codebook-only insider forges.** Possessing the codebook suffices if auth is a MAC.
**Mitigation:** Asymmetric signature (Ed25519) over the encoded payload, then signature+payload jointly encrypted under the codebook-derived pad and embedded. Outsiders see pure cover; insiders recover and verify. Verify keys are provisioned covertly, never published — Axiom 1.

**13. Stolen signing key (captured scout).** Perfect forgeries from the captured device.
**Mitigation:** Three stacked deterministic controls: (a) two-man rule — scout signature AND base-session countersignature both required; (b) per-key epoch window and message-count budget enforced by receiver-side monotonic counters; (c) freeze-on-miss — three missed check-ins triggers a covert revocation record (riding the channel as a normal instruction); frozen-key messages rejected unconditionally.

**14. Genuine-sender repudiation.** Real sender later claims "anyone could have built that."
**Mitigation:** Proof-of-authorship = signature + base's hash-chained, append-only log entry keyed by (epoch, seq). Log anchors periodically to multiple out-of-band custodians. Combined with secret verify keys, this yields designated-verifier semantics: provable inside, deniable outside.

**15. Downgrade / codec confusion.** Forced negotiation to a weaker legacy mode.
**Mitigation:** No negotiable crypto. Version byte pinned at provisioning; any other value → deterministic reject. Handshakes eliminated entirely — all parameters static per deployment, rotated out-of-band (handshakes are covert-channel liabilities anyway).

**16. Supply-chain codebook swap.** Poisoned distribution gives parties mismatched or weakened codebooks.
**Mitigation:** Codebook blob digest pinned in a dual-custodian provisioning ceremony; each message carries a codebook-generation byte; mismatch → deterministic drop plus alert on the separate channel.

**17. Burn-command forgery.** Fake "burn everything" to erase evidence selectively or DoS the pipeline.
**Mitigation:** Burn requires top-tier signature matching a pre-committed hash revealed at provisioning, confirmed by two consecutive authentic copies from different relays. Otherwise ignored.

---

## Class D — Burn-pipeline specific bypasses

**18. Resurrection via residue.** "Burned" plaintext persists in page cache, logs, snapshots, swap.
**Mitigation:** Decode and verify exclusively in locked pages (mlock); zeroize immediately post-verification; plaintext never touches disk — enforced as a CI grep gate over all serialized/logged forms plus a boot-time invariant. Single atomic deletion routine owns both body and metadata TTLs.

**19. Outbox capture.** Scout seized with queued outbound traffic.
**Mitigation:** Queue depth ≤ 1; items stored only as covertext; the pad share is deleted locally immediately on transmit-ACK. Exposure window bounded to one slot period by construction.

**20. Metadata outliving the body.** Routing records survive the burn and are the actual target.
**Mitigation:** Metadata shares the body's TTL and is deleted by the same atomic routine — no independent retention path may exist (asserted by storage-layer audit).

**21. Decoder oracle under injection.** Crafted covers crash the decoder or produce timing/error differences usable as an oracle.
**Mitigation:** Decoder is a total function: every input maps to valid-message or silent-drop, no on-wire error signaling. Constant-work decode — full decode+verify executes regardless of early failure, killing timing oracles. Fuzz gate in CI: zero crashes, branch-uniform timing profile on the adversarial corpus.

**22. Replay inside the validity window.** Context fields still fresh, so attack 10's cousin slips through.
**Mitigation:** Per-source sliding-window bitmap over sequence numbers; seen seqs dropped deterministically; window sized to maximum in-flight frames.

---

## Class E — Compelled disclosure and human layer

**23. Subpoena the codebook.** The sharpest deniability bypass: hand over the codebook and deniability dies, because there's only one decoding.
**Mitigation:** Dual-layer OTP by default. Construction: pick decoy P_d (auto-generated, contextually innocuous), random K_d, set C = P_d ⊕ K_d, then K_t = C ⊕ P_t. Distribute K_t to the parties; K_d sits where an adversary will find it. Same covertext decodes to the true message under K_t and a plausible decoy under K_d. Decoy generation is automatic per message — no operator discretion, no forgetting.

**24. Voluntary disclosure under capture.**
**Mitigation:** Duress template — a specific alternate "all-normal" report form whose use signals capture; receiver freezes all keys from that source on sight. Custody sharding: scout holds encode-capable material only, never the full decode side.

**25. Local side channels on the verifying device.** Power/cache observation during verification extracts key state.
**Mitigation:** Constant-time verify (no secret-dependent branches or memory access); dudect-style timing tests as a merge-blocking CI gate; secrets in secure element where hardware permits.

---

## Residual risk ledger (what no mitigation above covers)

Stated plainly, because pretending otherwise is how pipelines die:

- **Endpoint compromise pre-compose** — malware reading plaintext before encoding defeats everything downstream. Only answer is device hygiene, out of scope here.
- **Ambient-baseline drift** — if the cover model lags a shift in real traffic patterns, Class A protections decay. Weekly refresh is a bound, not a guarantee.
- **Global traffic analysis across many scouts** — per-message deniability doesn't defeat graph-level correlation over months. Constant-volume epochs blunt it; nothing eliminates it.
- **Base compromise** — the base holds verify keys and the log. Hash chaining and HSM custody raise cost; a sufficiently powerful base adversary wins. Two-man rule limits, not prevents.
- **Key custody is the whole game** — by design (item 6), confidentiality is information-theoretic, so every remaining attack reduces to stealing key material. Budget accordingly: the threat model collapses to "protect the keys," and every control above should be re-read in that light.

Enforcement rule, restated as the deliverable: each numbered mitigation ships as either a CI assertion (fingerprint match, no-plaintext-to-disk grep, fuzz/timing gates, label lint) or a runtime invariant (fail-closed version byte, anti-replay bitmap, ratchet abort, atomic TTL deletion). Anything neither machine-checkable nor runtime-enforced gets cut — prose mitigations are attack surface.
reasoning:
Let me parse this carefully. The user is asking about a "deniable-yet-verifiable comms protocol" — meaning a communication protocol where:

1. **Deniable**: The message can only be recovered with the codebook (i.e., to an outsider without the codebook, the content looks like noise or innocuous data — plausible deniability about what was transmitted).
2. **Verifiable/Authorship-provable**: The authorship of the message is provable (presumably to the intended recipient or auditor, using some key/signature mechanism).

This is in a "frontier-scout burn pipeline" context. Let me think about what that means. "Frontier-scout" suggests reconnaissance/exploration agents at the edge of a network or system — scouts operating in untrusted/hostile territory, sending back intelligence. "Burn pipeline" suggests messages are ephemeral — burned after reading, one-time use, no persistence. So this is like: forward scouts in contested territory send short-lived covert messages back; the pipeline burns them after consumption.

The user wants me to red-team this protocol: enumerate bypass attempts (ways an adversary could defeat either the deniability property or the verifiability property) and give deterministic mitigations for each.

Let me first formalize the protocol design space so my attack enumeration is grounded:

**Protocol components (assumed):**
- A codebook K shared between sender and receiver (this is the deniability key — needed to recover plaintext from covertext).
- An authorship key S (signing key held by the sender; verification key held by receiver/auditor).
- Cover traffic / steganographic embedding: ciphertext embedded into innocuous-looking carrier (e.g., timing patterns, image LSBs, header fields, padding, etc.).
- Burn semantics: after receipt/consumption, artifacts destroyed; possibly keys rotated per-message.

**Security goals:**
- G1 (Deniability/Confidentiality): Without K, an observer cannot distinguish carrier from random/innocuous traffic, nor recover content.
- G2 (Authenticity): With verification capability, the receiver can prove a given recovered message came from a specific authorized sender (non-repudiation among insiders), while outsiders see nothing verifiable.
- G3 (Burn/Ephemerality): Post-consumption, no residual artifact allows retroactive recovery or forgery.

The inherent tension: deniability usually wants repudiability (sender can deny), but here we want *authorship provable* — provable presumably only to those holding the verifier material. This is "undeniable to insider, deniable to outsider." Classic constructions: designated-verifier proofs, chameleon signatures, MAC-based authentication (MAC gives authenticity to key-holders but is deniable to outsiders since anyone with the MAC key could have forged it). Actually wait — if we want authorship provable, a plain MAC makes it forgeable by any key-holder, which weakens non-repudiation among insiders. The design likely uses asymmetric signature over the codeword, then embeds signature+payload via codebook into cover. Or uses a two-tier scheme: symmetric codebook for recovery/deniability, asymmetric sig for authorship.

Now, red-team: enumerate bypass attempts. Let me think adversarially across attacker positions:
- A1: Passive network observer (sees all traffic, no keys).
- A2: Active network attacker (can inject, replay, modify, drop).
- A3: Compromised endpoint (scout captured; has device, maybe partial keys).
- A4: Malicious insider with partial material (has codebook but not signing key, or vice versa).
- A5: Traffic analyst doing statistical detection (even without recovery, detecting *existence* of covert channel breaks deniability-in-practice).
- A6: Insider trying to frame someone (forge authorship).
- A7: Legitimate sender trying to repudiate after the fact ("I didn't send that").
- A8: Receiver-side compromise (burn pipeline leaks).

Bypass attempts against each goal:

**Against deniability (G1):**

1. **Statistical fingerprinting of the embedding channel.** If the codebook maps bits into cover features (e.g., LSBs, timing jitter, field values), naive embeddings leave distributional anomalies: LSB stego shifts histogram; timing channels show bimodal delays; padding lengths show non-uniform distribution. Deterministic mitigation: use a distribution-preserving encoding — map codewords onto cover symbols such that marginal and joint statistics match the natural cover distribution exactly (e.g., arithmetic-decoding-based steganography conditioned on a public cover model, or rejection sampling until feature vector matches empirical cover distribution within ε). Concretely: encode via arithmetic coding under a fixed model M trained on legitimate traffic; any bitstring decodes to a cover sample indistinguishable from M's output class. Also enforce uniform padding-length distribution by bucketing.

2. **Codebook reuse across messages → known-plaintext/correlation attacks.** If the same codebook entry or same keystream segment is reused, XOR-style reuse leaks: C1⊕C2 = P1⊕P2. Observer who obtains even one plaintext (via capture of a scout, or a leaked doc) can strip the pad from all overlapping traffic. Deterministic mitigation: per-message one-time pad derived from a ratchet: K_i = HKDF(K_{i-1}, nonce_i, "burn"), delete K_{i-1} immediately; never reuse any pad byte; nonce monotonic and unique; hard-fail on nonce collision (deterministic abort + key rotation).

3. **Length/volume correlation.** Message length in cover units correlates with plaintext length → metadata leak (traffic analysis recovers size, timing, cadence even if content hidden). Mitigation: fixed-size frames (constant-rate padding to canonical block sizes, e.g., always emit exactly N cover units per epoch, or quantize sizes to a small set matching benign traffic); deterministic: pad every payload to the next power-of-two bucket with PRF output, and add decoy epochs drawn from same PRF so total volume is constant regardless of load.

4. **Timing side channel.** Send-on-event reveals when events happen. Mitigation: time-sliced transmission — scouts transmit only at fixed slots (or Poisson with parameters identical to background chatter), buffering real payloads; empty slots carry PRF-generated dummy covers. Deterministic rule: emission times independent of event times (slot-quantized), verified by construction.

5. **Carrier selection bias.** If scouts choose unusual carriers (rare file types, odd ports), the mere choice flags them. Mitigation: restrict carriers to the population baseline — whitelist of carriers whose frequency in ambient traffic ≥ threshold; deterministic mapping from available carriers to this whitelist.

6. **Replay of old cover for correlation.** Attacker replays previously observed covertext segments to detect whether receivers act on them (behavioral oracle). Mitigation: epoch counters inside authenticated envelope; receiver deterministically drops anything with stale/non-monotonic counter before acting; no observable action on duplicates.

**Against verifiability/authorship (G2):**

7. **Signature stripping/re-embedding (cut-and-paste).** Attacker lifts a validly signed codeword from one cover and re-embeds it into a different cover/context to change apparent meaning (context substitution). E.g., "advance to grid X" signed once, replayed later when X is now wrong/harmful. Mitigation: bind signature to full context: sign (epoch, sequence, source-id, destination-id, carrier-hash, payload-hash). Receiver verifies all fields match current expected values; stale epoch → reject. Deterministic check list, fail-closed.

8. **Forgery via codebook-only possession.** Insider with codebook but not signing key tries to fabricate a message. If authentication were symmetric (MAC), they succeed. Mitigation: asymmetric signature (Ed25519) over the encoded payload; codebook alone insufficient. But note the tension: raw signatures are self-authenticating to *anyone* who sees them — if the signature is visible in the clear, it breaks deniability (an outsider sees a cryptographic blob proving something exists). Deterministic fix: encrypt the signature under the codebook-derived key along with payload (sign-then-encrypt-inside-cover), so outsiders see only cover; insiders recover both. Verification key distribution must itself be covert (pre-shared during provisioning, not fetched from public infra).

9. **Key-compromise impersonation / stolen signing key.** Captured scout's signing key lets adversary mint perfect messages. Deterministic mitigations: (a) two-man rule — require signature from scout key AND countersignature from base session key (both needed; capturing one party insufficient); (b) key usage limits: each signing key valid for a bounded epoch window and bounded message count, enforced by monotonic counters checked at receiver; (c) immediate revocation broadcast on loss-of-contact heuristic (scout misses 3 check-ins → its key frozen; frozen-key messages rejected deterministically). Note revocation broadcast itself must be covert — it rides the same channel as a normal instruction.

10. **Repudiation attack by genuine sender (the flip side).** Because the system promises deniability, a real sender may claim "that wasn't me — anyone could have made it." If authorship must be provable *among insiders*, need non-repudiation to the verifier set but deniability to outsiders. Deterministic construction: signature verifyable only with private verifier material (designated-verifier style): include in the signed transcript a trapdoor commitment V = Commit(payload, r) where r is chosen so that the verifier can also derive a fake transcript for any payload (DV signatures), OR simpler: keep the verification key secret (only base holds it) — outsiders can't prove anything because they lack both codebook and verify key; insiders can prove because base holds verify key and logs. The deterministic rule: verification keys never published; proof-of-authorship = signature + base's tamper-evident log entry keyed by epoch/seq.

11. **Malleability of the cover codec.** Some stego codecs allow transforming cover without changing extracted bits (e.g., JPEG recompression preserving LSB plane? No—lossy destroys LSBs; but format-transforming malleability: attacker converts PNG→BMP→PNG keeping pixel values, extracting same codeword, then re-signs? They can't re-sign without key, but they can *strip* the outer layer and re-embed the inner signed codeword into a new carrier — that's attack 7 again; covered by context binding including carrier-hash... careful: binding to carrier hash means the signer must know the exact final carrier bytes, which is awkward if embedding happens after signing. Deterministic order: pick carrier first, hash it, then sign (carrier-hash ∥ payload ∥ context), then embed. Embedding must be reversible w.r.t. untouched regions — use distortion-free embedding (e.g., modify only designated metadata fields whose values don't affect carrier-hash computation... circular). Cleaner: define carrier-hash over the invariant portions of the carrier (the parts not used for embedding), computed identically pre/post embedding. Deterministic spec: H = SHA256(carrier_invariant_bytes); sign(H ∥ ctx ∥ payload); embed into designated fields.)

12. **Truncation/splice attacks.** Attacker truncates a multi-frame message or splices frames from two messages. Mitigation: per-frame MAC/signature covering (epoch, seq, total-frames, frame-index, payload-chunk); receiver assembles only complete, contiguous, single-source sets; any gap → discard whole message deterministically.

13. **Downgrade/codec confusion.** Attacker forces negotiation to a weaker legacy codec (if handshake exists). Mitigation: no negotiable crypto — version pinned in provisioning; any version byte other than the pinned value → deterministic reject. Handshakes themselves are covert-channel risks; eliminate them: all parameters static per deployment, rotated out-of-band.

14. **Burn-pipeline specific: resurrection via backups/logs.** "Burned" messages persist in receiver logs, OS page cache, snapshots, or the scout's own outbox queue. An attacker who later compromises either end recovers "burned" content, breaking deniability retroactively (and enabling replay context study). Deterministic mitigations: (a) memory-only handling: decrypt/decode in locked pages (mlock), zeroize immediately post-verification; (b) no disk writes of plaintext ever — decode directly into verification buffer; (c) encrypted-at-rest everything else with per-boot keys; (d) deterministic scrub routine invoked on fixed schedule, plus on receipt of BURN command (which is itself an authenticated, covert-encoded instruction); (e) audit: any log line containing codeword fragments is a build failure — enforce via CI grep gate on serialized forms.

15. **Outbox queue theft on capture.** Scout captured with queued-but-untransmitted messages. Mitigation: store outbound queue only as covertext under ratcheted keys; capture yields covertext whose pad half is deleted after transmission (post-transmission deletion of the pad share — i.e., split pad: half generated at compose time kept on device until send, other half derived from ratchet state transmitted implicitly... hmm, simpler concrete scheme: outbound items encrypted with key K_i; K_i deleted locally immediately after successful transmit ACK; capture before send exposes at most the pending item — bound exposure window to seconds; deterministic: queue depth ≤1, flush interval ≤ slot period).

16. **Chosen-covertext injection (active probing).** Attacker injects crafted covers to make receiver decoder misbehave (crash → distinguishable error behavior; or decoder oracle leaking key material via error messages). Mitigation: decoder is total function — every input maps to either valid message or silent-drop; no error signaling on the wire, uniform timing for accept vs drop paths (constant-work decode: always run full decode+verify work regardless of early failure, to prevent timing oracles); fuzzing gate in CI requiring zero crashes and branch-uniform timing profile on adversarial corpus.

17. **Deniability collapse via metadata outside the carrier.** Even perfect cover fails if transport metadata betrays: destination IP rare, packet sizes odd, TLS fingerprint of custom client. Mitigation: tunnel through mainstream transport with standard fingerprints (e.g., domain-fronted HTTPS to popular CDN with stock client library versions pinned); deterministic lint: deploy config must pin client fingerprint string equal to current browser/lib release; test asserts fingerprint match.

18. **Insider framing via verify-key theft at base.** If base's verify key (or log) is compromised, attacker "proves" forged authorship. Mitigation: append-only tamper-evident log (hash chain, anchored periodically out-of-band to multiple custodians); verify key held in HSM, non-exportable; dual control for any export attempt (which should be impossible by policy enforced in firmware).

19. **Randomness failure.** Weak RNG on scout → predictable pads/nonces → recovery without codebook. Deterministic mitigation: hybrid randomness — nonce = SHA256(TRNG ∥ epoch ∥ counter); CI test vectors assert min-entropy floor; refuse to transmit if TRNG health checks fail (deterministic hold).

20. **Codebook extraction via many captured messages (codebook recovery attack).** If codebook is a static lookup table used repeatedly, an attacker collecting enough (cover, guessed-context) pairs can statistically infer the mapping, especially if cover model is learnable. Mitigation: codebook is not a table but a keyed pseudorandom function family: encode_i(m) = StegoEnc(HKDF(K, i), m) — per-message derived encoding; recovering any finite sample doesn't extrapolate (PRF security); rotate master K quarterly out-of-band; bound messages per master key (e.g., 2^20) with deterministic forced rotation.

21. **The "verifiable to whom?" leakage — verification oracle.** If receiver responds differently to valid vs invalid (e.g., ACKs valid, silent on invalid), attacker uses receiver as a signing/validity oracle to test forgeries offline-ish. Mitigation: uniform response policy — receiver emits statistically identical background traffic whether or not a valid message arrived (ACKs are implicit in next scheduled traffic, indistinguishable); deterministic rule: no observable state change correlated with validity.

22. **Substitution of the codebook itself (supply chain).** Adversary poisons the codebook distribution so a "shared" codebook differs between parties → comms fail (DoS) or worse, a weakened variant that attacker can read. Mitigation: codebook provisioned as fingerprint-checked blob: SHA256 pinned in dual-custodian provisioning ceremony; version byte inside each message references codebook generation; mismatch → deterministic drop + out-of-band alert through separate channel.

23. **Time-shift/reorder attacks within epoch.** Frames reordered → meaning altered if assembly order inferred from arrival. Covered partly by 12; explicit: sequence numbers signed per frame; assembly by seq, gaps fatal.

24. **Cover-model drift / steganalysis via ML.** Modern learned steganalysis detects even good embeddings when the encoder's cover model diverges from true cover distribution. Deterministic mitigation: generate covers *from* the same generative process as ambient traffic (not just "similar"): e.g., if cover is chat text, use the org's actual templated report generator seeded by codeword — covers are genuine-looking because they're produced by the genuine generator; the covert payload selects among generator outputs (choice-encoding). Choice-encoding sidesteps statistical artifacts entirely: every emitted cover is a fully valid generator output; information lives in the selection index. Deterministic guarantee: KL divergence between emitted cover distribution and ambient distribution is zero by construction (same sampler). Capacity lower, but sound.

25. **Burn-command forgery.** Attacker sends fake "burn everything" to disrupt (DoS on the pipeline) or to erase evidence selectively. Mitigation: burn command requires highest-tier signature and matches a pre-committed hash revealed at provisioning; execution gated on two consecutive authentic copies from different relays; deterministic.

26. **Partial-burn exploitation.** Pipeline burns message body but keeps routing records; routing metadata (who talked to whom, when, how much) survives and is the actual intel target. Mitigation: route records also padded/quantized and hashed-chain logged with same burn discipline; deterministic retention policy: metadata TTL = body TTL, enforced by single deletion routine that takes both atomically.

27. **Side channel on the decoder (power/cache on captured device during verification).** Local attacker observes verification to extract verify key or codebook state. Mitigation: constant-time verify implementation (no secret-dependent branches/memory); CI gate with dudect-style tests; secrets in secure element where hardware allows.

28. **Cross-protocol leakage.** Same codebook/key material reused in another protocol (e.g., also used for file encryption) creating cross-protocol oracles. Mitigation: domain separation strings mandatory in every HKDF call; lint enforces distinct labels; deterministic.

29. **Human-layer bypass: codebook written down / scout memorizes escape instructions.** Not crypto, but pipeline reality: capture leads to voluntary disclosure. Deterministic mitigations: duress codes — a specific alternate "all-normal" report template that signals capture (receiver treats subsequent traffic as hostile, freezes keys); sharded codebook: scout holds only the encode half sufficient for sending, not the decode half for receiving beyond minimal ACK parsing, limiting what capture yields.

30. **Replay within validity window.** Signed message replayed inside its own epoch (attack 7's cousin) — context fields still valid. Mitigation: per-source sliding-window anti-replay bitmap over sequence numbers; deterministic drop of seen seqs; window sized to max in-flight frames.

Also structural tension worth stating explicitly: **deniability vs. non-repudiation is a genuine tradeoff** — you cannot have public-verifiable non-repudiation and outsider-deniability simultaneously with the same artifact. The resolution is partitioned verifiability: authenticity provable only to holders of verifier material (base), invisible to others. State this as design axiom #1 because several attacks (7, 10, 18) exploit confusion about the verifier set.

And axiom #2: **every deterministic mitigation must be fail-closed and test-enforced**, otherwise "mitigation" degrades to guideline. Each mitigation above should map to a CI assertion or runtime invariant.

Now organize the answer. The user wants: enumerate bypass attempts + deterministic mitigation for each. Concrete, exact, grounded. I'll structure by attack surface with numbered bypasses, each with: the bypass mechanics (exact), why it works against the naive protocol, and the deterministic mitigation (exact mechanism, enforceable). I should also open with the two design axioms since they determine which mitigations are even coherent, and close with the residual-risk ledger (what remains unmitigatable — honest grounding: e.g., capture-with-torture bounds, endpoint malware before compose, ambient traffic baseline shift). Keep fluff out. Use headers and tight bullets. Length: substantial but dense — this is a hard problem deserving thorough treatment. Aim for maybe 1200-1800 words of dense content. Format: markdown with sections per attack class, numbered attacks, bold attack names, "Mitigation:" lines. Avoid tables probably — lists are better for this density. Actually a compact structure: Threat model assumptions briefly, axioms, then ~15-20 enumerated bypass/mitigation pairs grouped in classes, then residual risks. That's the shape.

Let me tighten the list to the strongest, most distinct bypasses (merge cousins):

Class A — Detection of the channel (deniability broken without recovery):
A1 statistical embedding fingerprints → distribution-matched/choice-encoding
A2 length & volume correlation → fixed buckets + PRF decoys
A3 timing correlation → slotted emission, buffered
A4 carrier/port/fingerprint outliers → baseline-whitelist + pinned transport fingerprint

Residual risks (honest): endpoint compromise pre-compose; ambient-baseline drift invalidating cover model; global traffic-analysis across many scouts; quantum future on recorded covertext (mostly moot if pads are info-theoretic — actually if OTP-ratchet, recorded covertext stays safe forever; note that as a deliberate property: make confidentiality information-theoretic via OTP so retroactive cryptanalysis is impossible, shifting all risk to key custody); insider at base.

That last point is strong: choose OTP-based confidentiality (information-theoretic) rather than computational crypto for the payload, so "recoverable only with our codebook" holds against *any* future adversary including unbounded ones — the only attack left is key custody. That's a grounded, exact design stance worth asserting.

One more bypass worth including: **the "two meanings" subpoena attack** — adversary with legal power demands the codebook; deniability requires ability to produce a *plausible alternative decoding*. If our scheme has only one decoding, handing over the codebook ends deniability. Deterministic mitigation: covertext constructed to be decodable two ways — primary codebook yields true message; a decoy codebook (provisioned separately, plausibly discoverable) yields an innocuous decoy message over the same bytes. This is the classic deniable-encryption requirement (Canetti et al.). Concretely: covertext = P_true ⊕ K_true = P_decoy ⊕ K_decoy arranged at provisioning time for planned decoys, or use the All-or-Nothing transform / double-pad construction: C = R ⊕ K_a; P_true = C ⊕ K_b where K_b looks random without K_b, and with decoy key K_d you get C ⊕ K_d = plausible decoy. Exact construction: choose decoy P_d and true P_t; sample K_d uniformly; define C = P_t ⊕ P_d ⊕ K_d... let me do it right: We want C such that C⊕K_t = P_t and C⊕K_d = P_d. Then K_t = C⊕P_t and K_d = C⊕P_d, so K_t⊕K_d = P_t⊕P_d. Provisioning: pick P_d (innocuous), pick K_d random, compute C = P_d⊕K_d, then K_t = C⊕P_t. Distribute K_t to sender/receiver, plant K_d where adversary will find it. Works per-message pair; needs pre-planned decoys or a streaming variant. Simpler operational version: every message carries a decoy layer by default (dual-layer OTP), decoy content auto-generated to fit context. Include this — it's the sharpest deniability-specific bypass (compelled disclosure) and most teams miss it.

Also **counter-forensic bypass: traffic absence analysis** — if messages stop when events happen (or scouts go quiet after big events), silence is signal. Mitigation: constant-rate heartbeat regardless of events; event info carried in content not cadence. Merge into A3.
